Chapter 6: Navigating Crisis and De-Escalation
As your relationship with someone living with BPD deepens, you might notice that moments of crisis can start to feel like part of the landscape. These aren't just everyday arguments or misunderstandings—sometimes, they're emotional earthquakes that shake up your world. Maybe it's a sudden outburst, a threat of self-harm, or someone pulling away without warning.
If you’ve ever felt completely thrown off by these moments, you’re not alone. Learning how to ride out these emotional storms—without losing yourself in them—is a skill that can really change the game, both for your own well-being and for the relationship itself.
So, what’s the first thing to keep in mind when a crisis hits? It’s all about knowing the difference between what’s truly urgent, and what isn’t. Not every emotional storm needs you to jump in and “fix” things right away. Sometimes, the best thing you can do is just stay calm and be present. That simple act can actually keep things from escalating, because you’re not fueling the emotional fire by reacting with panic or frustration.
Now, when you’re faced with a real crisis—like someone making threats of self-harm, or talking about hurting others—you absolutely want to take it seriously. But here’s the trick: don’t let yourself get swept up in the panic. Imagine you’re the anchor in the middle of a stormy sea. Your steadiness can mean the difference between things spiraling out of control, and bringing a sense of safety back to the moment.
So, how do you actually respond? Here are a few steps that can help:
First up, assess safety. If there’s a real, immediate risk, don’t try to handle it all on your own. Call in professional help, or reach out to emergency services. Your main job is to make sure everyone is safe—not to solve everything by yourself.
Next, stay grounded. Try taking slow, deep breaths, or repeating a calming mantra to yourself. These little things can help keep your own emotions in check, so you can actually be helpful in the crisis.
Then, set clear limits. It’s okay—actually, it’s healthy—to be clear about what you can and can’t do. For example, you might say, “I care about you, but I can’t help if you threaten me.” Setting that boundary isn’t selfish—it’s necessary.
Also, try to avoid arguing or lecturing. In the heat of a crisis, logic usually doesn’t land. Instead, focus on listening and letting the other person know you hear them, without getting pulled into a debate.
And don’t forget to follow up. Once things have calmed down, check in with both the other person—and with yourself. Ask, “What worked? What didn’t? How can I be better prepared next time?”
Let’s put this into a real-life situation. Imagine your partner, during an argument, threatens self-harm. Instead of panicking or making promises you can’t keep, you might say, “I’m really worried about your safety. I’m going to call someone who can help.” That response shows care, but also sticks to what’s realistic for you to handle.
Over time, having a personal crisis plan can make all the difference. Maybe you keep a list of emergency contacts handy, or work out a few phrases to use when you’re at a loss for words. And don’t forget to build in some self-care for after the storm passes—you need it too.
Remember, you don’t have to go through this alone. There are professionals and support networks ready to help when things get overwhelming.
Navigating crisis is really about finding that balance between compassion and boundaries. It’s about being present for someone else, without getting completely consumed by their emotions. It’s about choosing to respond thoughtfully, instead of just reacting. And every time you manage a crisis with steadiness and care, you’re building up your own resilience for whatever comes next.
